The transition from a 6.2 gram neonate to a 200 gram adult represents a greater than thirty-fold increase in mass, a growth trajectory that requires a substantial period of somatic development before reproductive maturity can be attained. Mating presumably occurs shortly after parturition in a post-partum estrus, though this has not been systematically documented for this particular species. The relatively low annual fecundity implies that each offspring must have a high probability of surviving to reproductive age to maintain stable population numbers, a demographic expectation that aligns with the species' occupancy of relatively stable grassland habitats rather than ephemeral or highly disturbed environments.
